title: The Berlin Ultimatum
description: It is August 1961. Soviet Premier Khrushchev has issued an ultimatum demanding Western powers withdraw from West Berlin within six months or face a unilateral Soviet peace treaty with East Germany. President Kennedy must respond without triggering open conflict.
question: How do you respond to the Soviet ultimatum over West Berlin?
optionA: Issue a firm public statement reaffirming allied commitment to West Berlin and place NATO forces on heightened readiness.
optionB: Request an emergency UN Security Council session to internationalise the dispute and buy diplomatic time.
optionC: Propose secret back-channel talks with Khrushchev, signalling willingness to discuss Berlin's status informally.
optionD: Withdraw a token number of troops as a gesture of de-escalation while maintaining the allied garrison.
impactA: NATO unity holds. Khrushchev backs down from the deadline but constructs the Berlin Wall weeks later as a face-saving measure. The West protests but does not intervene militarily.
impactB: The USSR vetoes the resolution, but the international attention stiffens allied resolve. The crisis simmers for months before a quiet understanding is reached.
impactC: The back-channel reduces immediate tension. Khrushchev interprets the secrecy as weakness and presses further concessions before agreeing to a tacit stand-off.
impactD: The withdrawal is read as capitulation. Domestic critics erupt. Allied partners question US resolve. Khrushchev presses his advantage in Vienna.

title: Taiwan Strait Flashpoint
description: China has conducted its largest-ever live-fire military exercises around Taiwan following a senior US congressional delegation's visit to Taipei. Regional allies are calling for US leadership. A carrier strike group is already in the Philippine Sea.
question: What is your immediate response to China's military exercises around Taiwan?
optionA: Order the carrier strike group to transit the Taiwan Strait as a freedom-of-navigation demonstration.
optionB: Issue a joint statement with Japan and South Korea condemning the exercises and calling for restraint.
optionC: Open a direct line to Beijing at the defence-minister level to signal that the exercises must cease within 48 hours.
optionD: Announce an acceleration of approved arms sales to Taiwan — F-16 upgrades and air-defence systems.
impactA: China labels it a provocation. The exercises intensify briefly before tapering off. The strait transit becomes a recurring flashpoint in bilateral talks.
impactB: The trilateral statement creates diplomatic cover and signals allied cohesion. Beijing protests but scales exercises back after five days.
impactC: Beijing agrees to a call. The 48-hour framing is rejected but exercises wind down in 72 hours. A back-channel is quietly maintained.
impactD: China condemns the sales and suspends climate cooperation talks. Taiwan gains meaningful defensive capability. Regional tension elevates to a new baseline.

title: The Martian Sovereignty Question
description: The year is 2047. Three corporate colonies on Mars — two American, one Chinese — have declared a joint provisional government and demanded recognition as an independent state under a newly drafted Martian Constitution. Earth's major powers are divided on how to respond.
question: How does your government respond to Mars's declaration of independence?
optionA: Recognise the Martian Provisional Government immediately, positioning your nation as the champion of self-determination.
optionB: Propose an interplanetary convention under UN auspices to negotiate a Martian status framework over two years.
optionC: Declare that existing treaty obligations mean the colonies remain under Earth jurisdiction and dispatch a legal mission.
optionD: Offer associate-state status — full internal autonomy, with Earth retaining authority over defence and resource export.
impactA: Your recognition triggers a cascade from smaller states. The major powers fracture. Martian stocks of rare isotopes become a bargaining chip in Earth politics.
impactB: The convention process is slow but builds legitimacy. The Martian government accepts the delay in exchange for observer status at UN bodies.
impactC: The colonies refuse the legal mission landing rights. The standoff becomes a PR disaster. Sympathy for Mars grows globally.
impactD: The associate-state model is adopted as a template. Mars gains effective independence within a decade through incremental renegotiation.

title: The Semiconductor Chokepoint
description: Your nation controls 60% of the world's advanced chip fabrication capacity. A rival bloc has begun stockpiling and is months away from closing the technology gap. Allies are pressing for export controls; trading partners warn of retaliation against your agricultural exports.
question: How do you leverage your semiconductor dominance before the window closes?
optionA: Impose immediate comprehensive export controls on all chips below 3-nanometre process to the rival bloc.
optionB: Negotiate a coordinated export-control regime with allied nations to prevent unilateral gaps from being exploited.
optionC: Offer a civilian-use licensing framework — chips for consumer goods permitted, military and AI applications banned.
optionD: Accelerate domestic stockpiling of critical materials while delaying any public export-control announcement.
impactA: The rival bloc retaliates immediately with agricultural tariffs. Chip prices spike globally. Allies complain they were not consulted.
impactB: Coordination takes three months but produces a unified regime with no loopholes. The rival bloc's development timeline slips by eighteen months.
impactC: The licensing framework is difficult to enforce. Diversion through third-party nations is detected within six months. Credibility suffers.
impactD: The delay gives the rival bloc time to secure alternative supply chains. When controls are eventually announced, their impact is halved.

title: Arctic Passage Dispute
description: Climate change has opened the Northern Sea Route year-round. Russia claims the passage as internal waters requiring transit fees. Three of your allied states' commercial vessels have been detained. The Arctic Council is deadlocked. Winter is approaching.
question: How do you respond to Russia's seizure of allied vessels in the Arctic Passage?
optionA: Escort the next convoy of allied commercial vessels with naval frigates, asserting freedom of navigation.
optionB: File a case with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea while negotiating temporary transit permits.
optionC: Propose an Arctic Passage Treaty — internationalising management under a new multilateral body with Russian co-leadership.
optionD: Offer to recognise Russian environmental regulation authority over the passage in exchange for releasing the detained vessels.
impactA: Russia backs down on the immediate detentions but doubles transit fees and increases coast-guard patrols. Tensions remain high.
impactB: The legal case takes years. The interim permits are granted at significant cost. The legal precedent ultimately favours your position.
impactC: Russia is initially sceptical but accepts co-leadership as a face-saving gain. A framework treaty is signed within eight months.
impactD: The detained crews are released. Russia interprets the concession as a precedent for further jurisdictional claims the following season.

title: Operation Blackout
description: Your signals intelligence agency has intercepted communications confirming a rival state's intelligence service is running three senior officials inside your government. Exposing them publicly would embarrass the rival but risk burning the source. A covert double-agent operation is possible.
question: How do you handle the discovery of a rival intelligence network inside your government?
optionA: Quietly arrest and prosecute the three officials under sealed proceedings, expelling the rival's station chief.
optionB: Turn one official into a double agent and feed the rival state controlled disinformation for six months.
optionC: Confront the rival government privately, demanding the operation cease within 30 days or face public exposure.
optionD: Share the intelligence with five allied counterintelligence services and coordinate a simultaneous exposure across all six nations.
impactA: The arrests disrupt the network. The expulsion triggers a reciprocal expulsion. The source is protected and remains active.
impactB: The double-agent operation succeeds for four months before the rival service grows suspicious and goes dark. Net intelligence gain is substantial.
impactC: The rival denies everything. Operations slow temporarily but resume through a parallel network. You have gained little and signalled your awareness.
impactD: The coordinated exposure embarrasses the rival globally. Two allied services uncover additional networks. The rival's foreign intelligence posture is set back by years.

title: The Pyongyang Calculation
description: North Korea has conducted its seventh nuclear test and is believed to have achieved miniaturisation for ICBM delivery. The regime is demanding formal recognition as a nuclear state and suspension of US-South Korea military exercises. South Korea is privately discussing its own nuclear deterrent.
question: How do you respond to North Korea's nuclear ultimatum?
optionA: Offer to suspend exercises for 90 days in exchange for a verifiable freeze on further testing and ICBM development.
optionB: Extend the US nuclear umbrella formally to South Korea and Japan in a public treaty with enhanced deterrence language.
optionC: Propose a six-party framework — US, China, Russia, Japan, South Korea, North Korea — to negotiate a phased denuclearisation roadmap.
optionD: Impose secondary sanctions targeting Chinese banks facilitating North Korean trade, pressuring Beijing to constrain Pyongyang.
impactA: North Korea accepts the freeze for 60 days then claims a violation and resumes. The exercise suspension creates a domestic backlash in Seoul.
impactB: South Korea and Japan publicly welcome the commitment. North Korea declares it a hostile act. China expresses concern about the treaty language.
impactC: China agrees in principle. Russia hedges. North Korea attends the first session and walks out on day two. The framework remains a useful diplomatic structure.
impactD: Three Chinese banks are sanctioned. Beijing retaliates with trade measures. North Korean smuggling routes shift but the economic pressure is meaningful.

title: Amazon Basin Emergency
description: An unprecedented drought combined with illegal burning has consumed 40% of the remaining Amazon rainforest over 18 months. The Brazilian government calls it an internal matter. Tipping-point scientists warn global carbon sequestration may be irreversibly compromised within six months.
question: How do you intervene as the Amazon approaches an irreversible tipping point?
optionA: Invoke the UN Framework Convention to request emergency Security Council authority for international intervention.
optionB: Assemble a coalition of 40 nations pledging a $200bn fund for forest restoration, conditional on Brazilian cooperation.
optionC: Announce immediate trade sanctions on Brazilian agricultural exports until deforestation rates drop below a verified threshold.
optionD: Offer Brazil a bilateral climate-debt swap — cancelling $15bn in sovereign debt in exchange for binding forest protection commitments.
impactA: Brazil's allies block the resolution. The debate takes three months. The forest continues burning. International attention does, however, shame Brazil into modest action.
impactB: Brazil accepts the framework. The fund is mobilised in phases. Deforestation slows by 60% within a year. The remaining 40% is harder to address.
impactC: Brazil retaliates with countersanctions. Domestic food prices rise in your country. Deforestation accelerates as the government rallies nationalist support.
impactD: Brazil accepts. The debt swap is ratified. Enforcement mechanisms are weak but satellite monitoring creates accountability. Forest loss slows significantly.

title: The Rohingya Tribunal
description: The International Court of Justice has issued a binding ruling requiring Myanmar to allow the return of 900,000 Rohingya refugees from Bangladesh. Myanmar's military government is non-compliant. Bangladesh is at capacity. Monsoon season is six weeks away.
question: How do you enforce the ICJ ruling and protect the Rohingya before the monsoon arrives?
optionA: Lead a Security Council resolution imposing targeted sanctions on the Myanmar military council and its commercial entities.
optionB: Fund and expand refugee infrastructure in Bangladesh for two years while building diplomatic pressure through ASEAN.
optionC: Recognise the National Unity Government of Myanmar as the legitimate authority and provide it with non-lethal support.
optionD: Convene an emergency pledging conference, securing $3bn in humanitarian funding and a burden-sharing arrangement across 12 states.
impactA: China and Russia abstain, weakening the resolution. Targeted sanctions are adopted but enforcement is patchy. The military council remains defiant.
impactB: ASEAN pressure produces a private Myanmar commitment to allow limited voluntary returns. Progress is slow but conditions in Bangladesh improve.
impactC: The NUG lacks territorial control. The recognition antagonises the military further. ASEAN partners express alarm at the escalation.
impactD: The burden-sharing arrangement holds. Twelve states accept defined quotas. The immediate humanitarian crisis is managed. The political question remains unresolved.

title: Grid Zero
description: At 03:00 GMT, a sophisticated cyberattack attributed with 90% confidence to a state-sponsored group has taken down power grids in three allied nations. Sixteen hospitals are on backup power. The malware variant matches a known toolkit. Attribution is solid but not yet public.
question: How do you respond to a state-sponsored cyberattack on allied power grids?
optionA: Release the full technical attribution evidence publicly and call an emergency NATO Article 5 consultation.
optionB: Deploy your offensive cyber capability to destroy the attacking group's command-and-control infrastructure immediately.
optionC: Share attribution privately with the suspect state, demanding restoration of the grids within six hours or face public exposure.
optionD: Convene an emergency Five Eyes session, harden allied grid infrastructure, and begin a covert counter-intrusion operation.
impactA: The public attribution galvanises allied support. The suspect state denies involvement. Article 5 consultations reveal disagreement on what constitutes an armed attack.
impactB: The offensive response is effective but triggers an escalatory counter-strike on financial infrastructure. Collateral damage in third-party systems is significant.
impactC: The suspect state denies involvement but quietly restores power to two of three grids. The private channel prevents escalation but sets a weak precedent.
impactD: The counter-intrusion succeeds in neutralising the attack infrastructure. Allies are hardened. The operation remains covert. Deterrence is re-established without escalation.
